It was a blend based on quality Brazil coffees, with a touch of aromatic Central American coffee to add a grace note to the cup, and it had a small percentage of premium robusta in it for crema, mouthfeel, and to add traditional flavors found on the continent. But times change and tastes change. Espresso culture is much less Euro-centric, and for good reason. While Italy gave us espresso, the general quality of your average espresso there can be quite poor. Don't even talk about coffee in France. The big brands in Europe are largely run by multi-nationals who keep a close watch on price, and gleefully buy lower quality green coffee if they can save .01 Euro. The privates follow suit, in order to compete. Of course, there are many exceptions, but the darker roast styles, well into 2nd crack, to cover up the use of low quality green coffee ... well, that is NOT something to emulate. For Sweet Maria's, espresso has never been our "dumping ground" for coffees we can't sell, old lots, or ones with mild defect. It's been a program where we have dedicated time, focus in cupping, and roast testing. With this in mind, we want to start over again, and offer New Classic, a somewhat silly name, an oxymoron, and overused ... but it says what I want it to say: Here is the new benchmark espresso with sweet-bittersweet balance, body, crema, and finesse, the core definition of the espresso beverage, and defines it in the established West Coast espresso style (clean, bright notes) without the burden of European espresso conventions. In other words, no robusta! Oh, and No obsessive interest in crema! (You can produce buckets of crema in espresso and still have a very mediocre-tasting cup. What ... do you make espresso just to look at the beautiful crema? No dummy, you make it to drink it!). New Classic generally involves Brazil as one of the base ingredients, with washed Centrals and South American coffees bolstering sweetness, and of course, chocolate roast tone. Blend ingredients will change with what's in season, but we always shoot for flavor continuity.
detail.short_description: A classic, balanced espresso, but without the baggage of the old world espresso conventions... and without robusta!

specs.Appearance: 1 d/300gr, 15-19 Screen - defect count will vary, but we're being on the safe side since the Monsoon coffee can have bug holes.

detail.full_cupping_notes: "Strange Beasts" bands together an unlikely coffee alliance that achieves a classic-toned espresso that leans heavily on balanced bittersweet flavors, and silky texture that's creamy and thick. We had excellent results at Full City roast level, and I wouldn't think twice about taking Strange Beasts to a rolling 2nd Crack if you enjoy the intensity of dark roasts. Like the king of the monsters, Godzilla, it can take the heat! It's versatile too, showing intense, long-lasting flavors with different throughputs (we enjoyed both our 1:1 ratio - 1:2 ratio shots). Deep cocoa flavors weigh heavily on the palate, thoroughly impressing a flavor of bittersweet bean to bar chocolate on the tongue. The flavors were very intense in this context, chalk full of cocoa roast notes, burnt sugars, and a very long finish. Notes of malt and date syrups add some sweetness to the deep-toned flavors, followed by pastry-like hints, bran muffin, and chocolate-covered almonds. The flavor profile branches out to modest fruit accents of raisin, dried fig, plum sauce, and a malty-sweet note of old fashioned date bread with a touch of molasses. Really though, it's the deep bittersweet intensity that holds this blend together, a key element that can be further developed with darker roasting. Longer shots that extracted closer to 30 grams of espresso over 30-35 seconds were still velvety in texture, and drew out the flavors of sweet breads drizzled in salty-sweet blackstrap molasses. We used a small amount of Monsoon coffee in Strange Beasts, which can settle to one part of your bag. Make sure to give it a quick shake/stir to evenly distribute before weighing out your roast batch.
detail.farm_notes:
Our Strange Beasts blend brings together an unlikely quartet of coffees with unique profiles. They coalesce to creamy, bittersweet flavors and balanced sweetness when brewed as espresso. Like the Japanese monsters ("Kaiju") we named the blend after, these improbable pairings pack a lot of punch... in a way that wouldn't be possible with any single component on its own.

So what are the strange beasts that make up this blend? We're not giving away too many specifics, but I can say that it's anchored by wet process coffee that brings impactful sweetness, while low-toned bittering and velvety body are boosted by small amounts of quality Robusta and Monsoon coffee from India. It also contains a dry process African component for flashes of fruit, bringing in a distinct profile in the context of the rest.

We've had a lot of fun tasting this blend at different roast levels and with multiple brew methods. Full City proved to be a great starting roast level—we really picked up on the sweet, caramelized hints this blend produces, along with roast-toned accents and notes of baked goods with fruit. Roasts taken to 2nd Crack become very pungent, bittering and intense, and will make a great base for milk drinks. Overall, we preferred espresso shots to brewed coffee, though I could see dark roasts working out well under full immersion brew methods, like French Press. No matter where you land, our classic-toned Strange Beasts blend is sure to find legendary status in your lineup!
detail.short_description: An unlikely coffee alliance yields balanced bittersweetness, well-integrated hints of fruit, baked goods, molasses, spice, and chocolate almond. Classic-toned, with velvety texture. Excellent straight or in milk drinks. Full City to French. Good for espresso.

detail.full_cupping_notes: * Limit 1 lb per customer. There's a lot we can learn from Project Alpha coffee. While "specialty grade" coffee we sell is prepared to a "zero primary defect" standard, Alpha is called R-400 because it has a minimum of 400 defects in 300 grams of coffee! Alpha is made up of wet-process Uganda arabica beans that are culled out during the processing and milling stages. It is sold only in full bulk containers to large commercial roasters who package and sell as pre-ground, instant or ready-to-drink coffee beverages. That is until now! We're offering small amounts of Alpha R-400 so that others can learn what's on the other side of the specialty coffee coin, offering a more holistic view of coffee's full range of quality. We found it fascinating to consider in visual context, and were surprised to find that it's actually quite interesting to taste too! Keep in mind that just because there's a lot going on in the cup, these aren't necessarily flavors we consider "desirable" in coffee. It's a coffee everyone should experience, but maybe not the one you'd reach for to drink. We have an article and video on how Project Alpha came to be in our Coffee Library . Roasted to Full City, the coffee smells of savory notes when ground, roasted nuts and grains, murky cocoa, and burnt Tamari. Pouring water on the grinds at first pulls out caramelized sweet accents, though quickly overshadowed by pungent earth notes when breaking the crust, potting soil and something like wet driftwood. The cup shares some features found in Robusta, intensely bitter, with layers of toasted grain and umami notes. However, it's a touch sweeter than Robusta, and has a lot more going on in the cup. There's some molasses up front along with dark caramelized hints, that lead into interesting spice and herbal accents, and a brothy Pho-like flavor starts to take shape. The cup really stretched our mental library of flavor references (especially for coffee!), touching on vegatal notes like artichoke and cooked broccoli, earthy raw cacao pods, whole spices, and a smokey chicory note that brought to mind New Orleans-style coffee. Good or bad, this is a complex tasting experience! For roasting, stick to City+ or darker, and expect oils on the surface after a few days rest no matter the roast level. (Alpha has a lot of lower density coffee, so it makes sense). We also noted a lower crack count, but it was audible in all our roast tests.
detail.farm_notes: We have an article and video on how Project Alpha came to be in our Coffee Library. We're carrying a small amount of Uganda "Alpha" commercial grade coffee so that our customers can experience this other side of specialty coffee production. It took a bit of convincing for our Ugandan supplier to agree to preparing this lot for us, and we're sure glad they did! It's been incredibly interesting to work with, and a source of many insightful observations around the office. We've found it surprisingly palatable at a medium roast level too, with flavors ranging from vegetal and food-like, to rustic-sweet and pungent. These aren't flavors we typically look for in coffee, but a thought-provoking exercise to taste and talk about nonetheless. While Uganda "Alpha" may sound like something pulled from science fiction, it's actually about as down to earth as coffee gets. This is low grade, "commercial" coffee, and the majority of coffee produced. Typically sold to large roasters and beverage companies, commercial coffee is roasted dark and sold packaged as a ground product, in pods, and in ready-to-drink beverages. And despite its prevalence in the marketplace, you don't typically get to see it in whole bean form because of the high number of defects. That makes this a rare opportunity to roast and taste commercial grade coffee yourself! The coffee is from Uganda, mostly grown in areas of Rwenzori and Mount Elgon, and sourced from the supplier we worked with for microlots this year. You might be surprised to find that Alpha coffee comes from many of the same farms that produced our microlots. Every farm produces low quality coffee, but it's removed during the milling process when preparing the top grades. This lot is prepped to what's called, "Alpha R400" in Uganda, which means it can have 400 primary defects per 300 grams of green (compare that to <1 primary defect in Specialty grade!).
detail.short_description: An opportunity to explore another side of coffee, infinitely interesting to see and taste. Earthy / root-like flavors with a touch of rustic sweetness, molasses, intensely bittering and pungent, roasted grains, chicory spice, cooked veggies. City+ to Full City+. *Limit 1 lb per customer.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Bugoye Muramba is an intense dry process coffee, pungent with roast tones and rustic sweetness, along with fruit characteristics in the light-to-medium roasts. The fragrance and aroma allude to dark chocolate-covered berry, with earth-toned sugars, like palm and date sugar, and fermented hints of red fruits and raw cacao. The cup has more of a dark, blackstrap molasses tone to the sweetness that provides a nice counterpart to the rustic elements. Fruits hint at the earthy side of dried prunes and dates, with jammy notes and plum sauce. There are some winey accents in the aftertaste that come off like honey mead and blackberry wine. We noted woody spices, whole allspice and cardamom, as well as piney incense cones. The coffee has potent roast bittering too, particularly when roasted to Full City or darker. The more developed roasts pull out rustic dark chocolate, bittering roasted cacao notes, and syrupy body.
detail.farm_notes: This coffee is a from a washing station in Bugoye town, part of the Rwenzori mountain range in Western Uganda. The station was built a few years back as part of a quality focused effort aimed at building smaller lots that focus on regional distinction. This is more challenging than you might think. Historically, Uganda was a supplier of large commercial blends, where volume, not quality, was the main objective. In contrast, these stations offer a competitive price as well as assistance to attract local farmers to deliver their cherry where it is centrally processed and separated into standardized grades. The Bugoye site sits at around 1200 meters above sea level, and while you see coffee growing in the area, most of it comes from the hills above between 1500 to 1800 meters. It's quite rural, and the higher hillside farms lack roads, leaving farmers to transport their harvest by donkey on foot. Farmers grow a mix of varieties, with SL-28 being quite common, along with SL-14, Costa Rica 95 and Catuaí (many are supplied by the owners of the washing station). This is their dry process coffee, which involves drying the whole cherries on raised beds with the seeds still intact. As you can imagine, it takes longer to dry whole cherries than just the coffee seeds, and the fermentation that occurs during this stage can impart fruit flavors in the final product. This lot has some of that strong fruit character that's a result of processing, but bittersweet roast tones find equal footing in the cup.
detail.short_description: Intense dry process coffee, pungent roast tones, rustic sweetness, accents of prune, blackberry wine, honey mead, rustic dark chocolate, syrupy body, woody whole spices in the long finish. City to Full City+.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Robusta coffees require a disclaimer for the uninitiated. Not only is it a coffee species distinct from Arabica, but the flavors lie in stark contrast too. Robusta coffees are intensely bitter, with low acidity, full body and savory complexity that add to its singularity. Robusta is also naturally high in caffeine, which makes them a favorite for espresso blends. We found this lot to be exceptional quality for Robusta, though still not for everyone! At Full City, the grinds let off dark-toned cocoa, bittering chocolate, with savory hints of toasted barley, umami notes. There's a pleasant hint of sweetness in the wet aroma, a rarity in Robusta coffee! We picked up on notes of sorrel, malted grains, with roast bittering, and cereal grains. The cup has incredibly thick body, which compliments the array of deep, chocolatey bass tones. Notes of Bakers brand unsweetened baking chocolate, and sharp cocoa powder have a strong presence in the cup, interspersed with toasted grain accents of puffed rice and wheat, roasted corn, and chocolate beer malt (especially aroma). There's a bitter clove oil note as the coffee cools, along with an herbal hint of dried tarragon. This is a very interesting coffee to taste, and one to try if you enjoy the intense, rustic character of Robusta.
detail.farm_notes: Masaka is located in Central Uganda, and quite a different coffee landscape than in the East where most of our coffee was sourced. Farms in this area are on a much larger scale than the smallholder farms in Mount Elgon region, and lower altitude too. The low altitude and warm climate are a big part of the reason this area is predominantly planted in Robusta. Low altitude is not something we talk about much in coffee, mainly because the Arabica species - most of what we buy - does poorly in those conditions because of susceptibility to pests, fungus and diseases. Robusta, however, is an entirely different coffee species (Coffea canephora), and thrives in low, hot regions. Robusta has a naturally high caffeine content, which offers resilience to the problems that plague Arabica. Robust as it may be, cup quality is the big trade-off. Robusta is typically bitter, with low acidity, thick body and best roasted dark. As a result, it's a cheaper option than Arabica coffee making it a favorite base ingredient for many commercial coffee blends. In recent years there's been a growing interest and demand for "Specialty" Robusta - that is, Robusta that's been processed with the same care and attention as Arabica. The cup certainly benefits from it, but there's no shaking the intense bittering, and grainy accents that are unique to Robusta. It's incredibly interesting to taste, and this lot is certainly one of the better Robusta coffees we've picked up. It was dry processed, meaning the whole cherry is dried with the seed still intact. This style of process method can sometimes impart fruit flavors in the cup, though that's not the case here. I think it lends some lightly sweet accents though, which are often lacking in Robusta coffee.
detail.short_description: Intense flavors, unsweetened baking chocolate, sharp cocoa, toasted grains, puffed wheat, roasted corn, chocolate beer malt, bitter clove oil, dried tarragon, low acidity. Full City to French. Good for espresso blending.

overview_attrs.Cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids

detail.full_cupping_notes: This is a very clean smelling coffee, with sweet notes of raw sugars, vanilla malt, with subtle spice accents of clove and Root Beer. Pouring the hot water on the grinds brought out more profoundly sweet notes of brûlée sugar, ginger snap cookies, and almond brittle candy, with just a hint of black tea when breaking through the crust. City/City+ roasts bring balanced sweetness to the cup, showing creamy caramel notes, dark toffee, and raw turbinado sugar. Bright hints of ripe lemon, and zested peel highlight this coffee's sparkling acidic impression, though it stays pretty well-integrated with the sweetness. The cup cools to faintly tart accents of dried goji berry, lemon tea, and a haze of cocoa in the aftertaste. Overall, the flavors are balanced and very well-structured, and I found myself comparing the cup to some of our Antiguan Estate coffees. I'm sure dark roasts will perform well too, but we haven't found a reason to roast this coffee any darker!
detail.farm_notes: Kapchorwa was one of the highest elevation stations we visited on our 2025 visit, and sits right around 1950 meters above sea level. Most of the coffee they buy is from high elevation zones by proximity, and the quality of cherry selection and parchment caught our eye. They currently have around 1000 farmers registered with the station, allowing them to track granular details about things like quality delivered, farmer payments, and outreach. Most of the farmers in the region grow a mix of varieties, with SL-28 being quite common, along with SL-14, Costa Rica 95 and Catuaí (many are supplied by the owners of the washing station). They use a water conserving Penagos pulper to process the coffee, ferment it for around 12 hours to break down the mucilage, and then wash away the remaining fruit with water in tile channels. The coffee dries on raised beds for around 12 days, and is finished in a mechanical dryer.
detail.short_description: Light roasts brew balanced sweetness and structured flavors. Sweet notes of creamy caramel, dark toffee, and raw sugar, along with hints of lemon and dried goji berry that highlight acidity. City to City+.

specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 14+ screen - I'm grading conservatively to temper expectations. It's a really nice sort for Yemen, however you may see a few quakers, broken beans and minor bug holes.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Khulani has unique fruit-accented flavors that are intensely rustic and bittersweet. The smells at City+ and Full City roast levels have very nice roast intensity, pungent and bittersweet, with notes of burnt sugar, toasted grains, and brown rice syrup. I really enjoyed the interplay of pungent caramelized sugars and savory nut smells in the wet aroma, accented by hints of fruit leather, cooked sweet squash, and aromatic wood. The base flavor profile has fruited bittersweetness, like freeze dried berry with bittering cocoa, flanked by earth tones and savory spice accents. My City+ roast showed notes of rustic sweeteners, sorghum and dark corn syrups, with toasted grains, pumpkin bread, and a powdery fruit aspect like banana protein shake. Like all Yemeni coffee, it carries an intense, earthy side that can be polarizing. Flavors of tanned leather, dried Cumin and Coriander, fresh cut wood, and chicory are interesting, to say the least, but not for everyone. Darker roasts pulls out layer upon layer of bittersweet cocoa characteristics too, along with a hint of dried date, and an underlying foresty aroma that lingers.
detail.farm_notes: "Khulani" is the name given to heirloom cultivars selected and cultivated in the Khulan Amer district, Sa'ada. Generally, this is a varietal distinction based on regional cultivation, and includes a subset of varietal types that are dispersed across 6 districts in the Sa'ada Governorate. This particular lot comes from a farmers association in the region called the Khulani Coffee Society for Agricultural Development, who's mission has been to improve both quality and productivity for coffee farmers across the surrounding regions by offering technical support and price stability through their relationships with marketing agents. The coffee is collected from small farmers in the Sana'a mountain growing regions of Saqin, Haidan, Joma'ah Razih, Munabbeh, and Ghamer. To get slightly more granular, 222 farmers in total contributed coffee from their farms to this regional blend, who on average have 1000 trees planted on less than 1/2 hectare of land. Coffee is grown at extremely high altitudes, starting at 1400 meters and topping out at 2500 meters above sea level! This lot was secured through Fatoum Muslot, who runs the family coffee business, Pearl of Tehama, started by her father back in the 1950s. They've long exported Yemeni coffee, and since Fatoum has started managing the group, she has worked to implement practices such as more stringent hand sorting and using Ecotact storage bags in order to directly affect their coffee's overall quality. We're quite pleased with the physical condition of both coffees we bought from Fatoum this year, the lack of underripe coffee and shipping in barrier bags has really benefitted the resulting cup quality. During their long history in the coffee trade they've forged longstanding connections with farming groups in several growing regions, and because of these connections, are able to buy coffee in a more direct way.  This It's been a few years now since we've picked up Yemeni coffee, not necessarily by choice, but mainly due to the difficulties exporting from a country at war. The situation there is still quite dire, and I'm amazed that anything is making it out of the country. Read our interview with Fatoum Mouslot from 2020.
detail.short_description: Fruit-accented profiles, intensely rustic and bittersweet coffee, notes of dark corn syrup, toasted grain, pumpkin bread, freeze dried fruit, leather, Cumin, bittering chocolate. City+ to French. Good for espresso.

specs.Region: Haima Dakhliya, and Kharijea Districts, Sana'a governorate
specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 14+ screen - I'm grading conservatively to temper expectations. It's a really nice sort for Yemen, however you may see a few quakers, broken beans and minor bug holes.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Haimi has a unique spiced dimension, and otherwise fits right in with the rest of our Yemeni coffees; deep-toned, earthy, and appropriately rustic. The grinds show earthy-sweet notes of palm sugar, savory hints of unsweetened cocoa and roasted peanut. Baking spices imbue the wet aroma, along with malted chocolate and leafy Yerba Mate. City+/Full City is a good roast range to start with, where deep-toned flavors are pungent, and complex spice notes bring out interesting profiles of baked goods. Heady spices like fenugreek and Allspice add complex layers to the aroma and drawing out hints of saffron cookie, fennel sweet bread, sesame and pistachio. Rustic notes of rice syrup, leather, and tobacco are underpinned by syrupy dark cocoa that lends to some bittering aspects in the finish. Darker roasts that hit 2nd Crack have their own appeal, rooty and tangy with roast, with waxy body that stands up to steamed milk. It's made a great espresso shot, even as a lighter, City+ roast. I was floored by the thick, creamy texture, and intense bittersweet flavors of high % cacao content chocolate, toasted nibs, sesame oil, and a subtle note of freeze dried fruit.
detail.farm_notes: Haimi is a distinct regional coffee, but has often been sold as Sana'ani since it is geographically contiguous with the area around the capital, Sana'a. Many moons ago, I found a Yemeni exporter willing to separate the Haimi (he refers to it as Haima: Haimi simply means "of Haima"). I found it's unique cup character appealing, and it seemed to have a dark sweetness that was distinct from our other Yemeni offerings. Now we are working with another Yemeni exporter, who is separating coffee regionally from Haima Dakhliya, and Kharijea Districts in Sana'a governorate. This lot is made up of coffees from about 100 different farmers, most with less than 1000 trees planted. There's a great range in altitude, and coffee grows is areas as low as 1000 meters above sea level, all the way up to 2000 meters. Read our interview with Fatoum Mouslot from 2020.
detail.short_description: Baking spice notes make a strong showing, along with classic Yemeni flavors that are deep toned, earthy, and appropriately rustic. Fenugreek, saffron cookie, sesame oil, tangy roast flavors. City+ to French. Good for espresso.

specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 13+ screen - I'm grading conservatively to temper expectations. It's a nice sort for Yemen, however you may see a few quakers, broken beans and minor bug holes.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Sanani has the kind of intensity that's unique to Yemeni coffee, rustic and bittersweet flavors vying for equal footing in the cup, and body that's about as thick as coffee gets! The fragrance of the ground coffee has intense spice and burnt sugar notes, accented by potent notes of dried fruit and cherry wood. The wet aroma had a fruit syrupy note, with Chai spice, coriander, dark roasted cacao nibs and something like charred cedar. The cup flavors covered similar ground, bittersweet and a little fruity, with woody spices and earth-toned characteristics up and down the different roast levels we tested. Medium roasts are very thick-bodied, with layers of rustic palm sugar, dried fruit hints and a complex earth-toned aroma that's both spiced and savory. The cup sweetness has elements of burnt brown sugars and barley malt syrup, accented by notes of toasted pumpkin seeds and saffron cookie. The profile opens up to fruited hints, like natural dried apricot and prune, and the spiced elements take on more of a woody dimension - think whole cloves and cinnamon sticks, with a bit of woody incense in the aftertaste. You can really drive up the deep, chocolate-toned flavors in the dark roasts, and the finish seems to last forever no matter the roast level! All roasted coffee benefits from resting, but we find this to be particularly true for Yemeni coffee. Best with 72 hours+ rest.
detail.farm_notes: This regional Yemeni blend, "Sanani", is from small-holder farmers in the broader Sana'a region. This lot was secured through Fatoum Muslot, who took over the family coffee business started by her father back in the 1950s. They've long exported Yemeni coffee, and since Fatoum has started managing the group, she has worked to implement practices such as more stringent hand sorting and using Ecotact storage bags in order to directly affect their coffee's overall quality. We're quite pleased with the physical condition of both coffees we bought from Fatoum this year, the lack of underripe coffee and shipping in Ecotact liners has really benefitted the resulting cup quality. During their long history in the coffee trade they've forged longstanding connections with farming groups in several growing regions, and because of these connections, are able to buy coffee in a more direct way. This lot is made up of coffee from roughly 300 farmers Sana'a, who on average have 1000 trees planted on less than 1/2 hectare of land. Altitude is extremely high, starting around 2000 meters and stretching upwards of 2400 meters above sea level. Read our interview with Fatoum Mouslot from 2020.
detail.short_description: Intensely rustic, bittersweet flavors, lightly fruited, with body that's about as thick as coffee gets. Barley malt syrup, earthy dark chocolate, natural dried fruits, saffron cookie, fragrant wood and spices. City+ to French. Good for espresso.

detail.full_cupping_notes: We don't get coffee from Cameroon all that often, so it's a rare opportunity to try this lot of Java cultivar produced in Kouoptamo. The cup is bittersweet and roast-toned, not too flashy, though it does have interesting hints of fruit and toasted grain, and citrus-y acidic hint. The dry fragrance and wet aroma had hints of praline nuts, honey wheat bread, malted barley sweetness, banana chips, and pipe tobacco. The cup produces a very pleasant roast taste in the City+/Full City levels, nut toned filberts, bittering cocoa, along with an accent of toasted coconut in the finish. It offers sweet hints of molasses cookie and rice syrup, with balanced brightness that draws out accent notes of earthy Matcha tea, and lemon bars. Both of our medium roasts had viscous body that was somewhat oily in texture, leading to a very long finish.
detail.farm_notes: Cameroon is an interesting origin in the Specialty Coffee terms. For starters, this is West African coffee, not East African like most other arabica offerings such as Kenya, Zimbabwe, Rwanda. And a large percentage of Cameroon coffee has traditionally been robusta, grown in all provinces except the north, while arabica is mainly produced in the high altitudes of the west, northwest and east. The western highlands of Cameroon, where much of the coffee is grown, averages about 5,000 feet above sea level and has two distinct seasons, the rainy season and dry season, which benefits quality arabica. This lot is from the Grassfields Cooperative, located in the Bamenda Plateau region. However, this lot is from small holder farms in Kouoptamo, not too far from the mountainous Bamboutos region. The cooperative produces both wet and dry process coffees, and this is the former. They depulp coffee into tanks where it ferments for up to 36 hours to break down the sticky fruit mucilage, which can then be washed away with clean water. Coffee is dried on raised beds for around a week to 10 days. Most of the coffee is grown around 1000 to 1200 meters, and you see a lot of Java and Jamaica varieties planted in Cameroon. I want to mention that we've found a few lentils and seeds in this coffee in previous years. It's not all that uncommon in coffee since they often share the same drying patio. Some mills are better than others at getting it out, but it does come with the territory. We removed what we spotted by hand, but expect that one or two may make it through our own screening every now and then.
detail.short_description: The cup is bittersweet and roast-toned, with hints of brown rice syrup, filbert nut, toasted coconut, lemon bars, earthy Matcha. A rare opportunity to try coffee from Cameroon. City+ to Full City+.

specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 15-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination

detail.full_cupping_notes: *We located 100# of this earlier 2026 lot of EA decaf and are offering it at a discount. The dry grounds show balanced sweetness of light brown sugar, milk chocolate, and a hint of dried apple. Hot water brings up a bit of pumpkin spice bread, dusted with dark cocoa powder. This brews such a well-rounded cup at City+ roast level. The profile is highlighted by raw sugar sweetness, with a hint of fruit that adds to a pleasantly moderate level of acidity. Base flavors hint at grain sweeteners, like barley malt, with a note of wheat toast with honey. It strikes a nice balance of sweet and bittersweet flavors as it cools, and a faint dried apple note brings a lively aspect to this roast level. It should definitely take to darker roast levels to, though we haven't roasted many batches beyond Full City at this point. EA decafs tend to have good body for carrying roast tone well, and this lot is no exception.
detail.farm_notes: This decaf blend comes from several small farms in Colombia's Southern Department of Huila. Colombia's coffee growing communities are largely made up of what are considered "small producers", with close to 95% managing 5 hectares or less. These are typically wet processed coffees, using small pulping machinery at home, fermented to remove the outer mucilage layer, then dried inside small drying rooms that help protect the coffee from the elements. The coffee is decaffeinated right in Colombia. The plant is called Descafecol, located in Manizales, Caldas. It's a state-of-the-art facility, partly owned by Coffein Compagnie from Germany. The method used is direct contact type using Ethyl Acetate, which can be naturally derived from fruits and vegetables, thus is generally referred to as a natural decaf method (often called "sugar cane decaf").
detail.short_description: *We located 100# of this earlier 2026 lot of EA decaf and are offering it at a discount. Well-rounded cup profile with balanced bittersweet flavors and just a hint of fruit that lends to the acidic impression. Notes of barley malt, honey on toast, dried apple, dark cocoa. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.

detail.full_cupping_notes: At City+ roast level, the dry fragrance presented an underlying note of blackstrap molasses that laid out a nice background for contrasting hints of leathery dried fruits, and pungent roast bittering. The wet aroma smelled resinous and sticky-sweet with a scent of caramelized sugars, like caramel cooking in a pan, with some stewed fruits behind it and winey berry accents. The cup shows really nice bittersweet intensity in the light and middle roasts we tested. It has a pungent, deep-toned core that connects to some really interesting accents of fruits and light herbal notes. City+ roasts brought out hints of canned plum, unsulfured apricot, with dark fruits that have a winey ripeness to them. Full City was inky and low toned, with layers of dark chocolate and earthy cacao, cooked dark fruits, and heavy mouthfeel. A lot to offer at both ends of the roast spectrum.
detail.farm_notes: This coffee from Hacienda Sonora is part of a family operation that goes back five generations in Costa Rica's West Valley region. The Guardia family have farmed coffee here for more than 100 years, historically selling their harvest to large mills, as was the norm. That all changed in the late 90's with the micro-mill revolution that swept Costa Rica, and, seeing value in controlling their coffee quality through to export, the family erected their own small milling operation at their farm. Currently under the management of Diego Guardia, the farm have decided to move away from more water intensive process methods, favoring honey and dry process instead. This 18 bag lot is considered a "yellow honey", in that roughly 50% of the fruit mucilage is left intact after depulping, and isn't removed until after the coffee is fully dried (to 10-11% moisture). This process method can impact the cup flavors and physical characteristics too. In the case of this coffee, it possesses fruit and wine-like notes, big body, no doubt tied to process method. The beans also look a little darker when roasting, and produce more chaff, both due to the fact that the seeds have more silver skin than a fully washed, wet process coffee. Hacienda Sonora sits at 1300 meters above sea level, and is planted in a variety of cultivars, including this "Centroamericano" separation, which is a first generation hybrid with some resistance to leaf rust. We also purchased a fully natural (dry process) lot from Sonora that comes later in the year.
detail.short_description: Pungent bittersweetness connects to interesting accents of fruits and light herbal notes. Canned plums, unsulfured apricot, dark fruits with a winey ripeness, long bittering notes, pronounced body. City+ to Full City+.

detail.full_cupping_notes: The fragrance has a rustic intensity that is both bittersweet and fruited, with notes of cacao nibs, fermented fruits, and a Ricola-like herbal accent. Fruity profiles are a bit more apparent in the wet aroma, where intense fruit notes emanate from the wetted crust, pulpy, with a hint of winey ferment, sticky dried apricot, along with dark cocoa powder. The cup offers pungent dark-toned bittering, with a range of rustic fruit accents, and impressive roast intensity, particularly when roasted to Full City and darker. City+ roasts had notes of chocolate-covered dried fruits, with accents of honey mead wine, coconut palm sugar, dried prune, and fermented orange. The fruits bring about a slight acidic impression in the lighter roasts, though fairly mild in comparison to the rest. I brewed a batch in my V60 after 3 days' rest and thought the fruit aspects settled down a bit, and were more integrated in the bittersweetness. The cup aroma was also enticing when drinking it, and offered glimpses of cinnamon bark, raisin, and cherry wood as it cooled.
detail.farm_notes: The 120 manzana Finca Miravalles is a family affair. It's owned by husband and wife Luis Duarte and Tete Chacón, and much of the management is handled by their son, Luis Jr, and Chico, the on-site manager of 15 years. The farm is located in Apaneca, Ahuachapan, not too far from the Santa Ana volcano. It used to be two separate farms, Miravalles belonging to Tete's family, Santa Maria to Luis's. They were both raised on these neighboring farms, family ownership going back some 150 years. Sometime after marrying, they put in an offer on Miravalles, which was all but abandoned at the time, and joined with Santa Maria under the Miravalles name. They have been renovating the farm ever since, keeping much of the original Bourbon and Pacas cultivars, and planting several other varieties, including H1 and F1 hybrids, Catimor, Pacamara, Caturra, and Gesha. They've done an amazing job segregating the cultivars in separate plots, and go to great lenghts to harvest and process separately too. This year we bought several of the varietal separations, this being an all Cuscatleco lot (disease resistant sarchimor). It's also a dry process coffee, which in general terms means they dry the whole coffee cherries with the seeds inside, rather than removing first. There's an additional step to the dry process method at Miravalles, which first involves sealing up in plastic bags for 3 days during which the cherries ferment. Then they pour the cherries onto raised beds where they dry for around 2 weeks. The resulting cup is quite fruit forward, big bodied, and with fairly low level of acidity. Miravalles is perched on the verdant slopes of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec mountain region, and spans an altitude range of about 1250 to 1550 meters above sea level. Check out our video tour of the Miravalles farm , and in-depth look at their wet process method in action at their mill.
detail.short_description: Pungent dark-toned bittering with a range of rustic fruits, and enticing cup aroma. Palm sugar, dried prune, cacao nibs, honey mead, cinnamon bark, cherry wood. City to Full City+.

detail.full_cupping_notes: The fragrance of the grinds was layered with unrefined sweetness and bittersweet accents, barley malt syrup, dark molasses, torched sugar, and dried date. I sensed a bit more fruit in the wet aroma, like fruited chocolate, along with notes of dried papaya and earthy figs. City+ and Full City roasts show quite a bit of roast intensity in the brewed coffee; bittering cocoa, burnt caramel, countered by a winey aroma that brings to mind dessert wine, like Sherry. The flavors are pungent and complex, with notes of rustic Oaxacan chocolate, baking cocoa, and a savory hint of toasted sesame. Accent notes of berry fruit leather and preserved orange slices crop up in the cup, and a briney aspect marks the aftertaste. It can be quite a pungent coffee, the bittersweet roast flavors overtaking the cup in medium-to-dark roasts. City+ is where you'll find more of that interplay of natural dried fruits and rustic bittersweets that we really enjoyed.
detail.farm_notes: The 120 manzana Finca Miravalles is a family affair. It's owned by husband and wife Luis Duarte and Tete Chacón, and much of the management is handled by their son, Luis Jr, and the on-site manager of 15 years named Chico. The farm is located in Apaneca, Ahuachapan, not too far from the Santa Ana volcano. It used to be two separate farms, Miravalles belonging to Tete's family, Santa Maria to Luis's. They were both raised on these neighboring farms, family ownership going back some 150 years. Sometime after marrying, they put in an offer on Miravalles, which was all but abandoned at the time, and joined with Santa Maria under the Miravalles name. They have been renovating the farm ever since, keeping much of the original Bourbon and Pacas cultivars, and planting several other varieties, including Icatu variety . They've done an amazing job segregating the cultivars in separate plots, and go to great lenghts to harvest and process separately too.Miravalles is perched on the verdant slopes of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec mountain region, and spans an altitude range of about 1250 to 1550 meters above sea level. Check out our video tour of the Miravalles farm , and in-depth look at their wet process method in action at their mill.
detail.short_description: Pungent dry process with intense bittersweet flavors, countered by rustic fruits and a winey aroma. Notes of fruit leather, preserved orange, toasted sesame, burnt caramel, Sherry, Oaxacan chocolate. City+ to Full City+.

specs.Region: Gerba Dogo, Bule Hora, Guji Zone

detail.full_cupping_notes: Anaerobic processing has certainly left its mark, however, not in a full-on "boozy" fruit kind of way. The cup profile is packed with interesting fruit flavors and ripe aspects are balanced by supportive sweetness and delicate aromatic highlights. The fragrance has a mix of fruits and chocolate, with ripe, winey accents of fermented grapes and berries, and hints of fragrant spices. Pouring hot water on the grinds enhances the fruited sweetness, and takes on delicious smelling jammy tones, blackberry and peach, along with some subtle accents of fermented fruits, and spiced berry compote. The hot cup has a ripe peach note that shifts to cooked berry reductions, with hints of green melon. The cup aroma has a slight floral dimension that becomes more resinous as the coffee cools, like fresh hops and rue herb, along with an oaky rum accent in the finish. Full City pulls out some bittersweetness from the otherwise fruited cup, with dark-toned cocoa that has a bit of bittering to it. There's really nice fruit undertone to the dark roasts, berry-toned and a little pulpy, and comes together like fruit liqueur chocolates.
detail.farm_notes: The lot was processed at the Gerba Dogu mill (sometimes spelled "Gerba Doku"), not far from Gerba town, in Ethiopia's southern Guji Zone. Gerba Dogu is run by Gemechu Shonora, along with brothers Shebura, Morkata and Adugna. Their father worked for the local union many years ago as a coffee collector, going out into the surrounding towns buying coffee cherries from farmers. The processing site sits at 2200 meters above sea level, and some of the farms they buy from are even higher elevation. Historically, they've produce dry and wet process coffees, and more recently started experimenting with anaerobic and honey processing as well. This is an Anaerobic Natural, which essentially involves storing the whole coffee cherries in air tight containers for a few days before laying to dry on raised drying beds. This added step seems to have enhanced flavors of berries and fruits in the cup, at times winey, and always sweet. The cups we brewed were quite aromatic too, slightly floral with resinous herbal accents. They typically dry these coffees in the sun for 3 days, and then an additional 2+ weeks in the shade to help the seeds to stabilize a bit. There are some pretty small beans in this lot, but thankfully not so small that you need to worry about roasting in the grid drum of a Behmor.
detail.short_description: Ripe fruits are balanced by supportive sweetness and delicate aromatic highlights. Complex profile of berry compote, peach jam, fresh hops, rue, winey accents of oaky rum and fruit liqueur chocolates. City to Full City.

detail.full_cupping_notes: There's a sweet scent of caramel and chocolate in the grinds, with dried berries and fragrant baking spice accents. The wet aroma smelled of chocolate-dipped berries, strawberry drizzled in honey and a jammy blackberry note raised in the steam. Korate shows very nice fruit tones in the cup, especially in light to medium roast levels. I've enjoyed sitting with this coffee and observing the shifting flavor profiles as it cools, from fruits and berries, to chocolate bittersweets, and aromatic hints in the nose. Flavors of rustic sugars are accented by dried peach and blueberry, with some pungent burnt sugars filling out the finish. City roasts have a juicy aspect, cranberry with a splash of lemon, along with tangy red tea that brings on a moderate acidic impression. The aroma has herbal notes of fresh mint and lemongrass, with baking spice suggestions. It works great at medium-dark roast levels too, developing depth to the bittersweet tones that come together with dark fruit hints. Full City brewed flavors of chocolate truffles with raspberry swirl, raisiny dried fruits that mingle with a sharply bittersweet aftertaste.
detail.farm_notes: This lot was processed at a privately run coffee processing site called Korate (also the name of the village), very near to Dari Kidame area, in Western Guji. The farmers who deliver to the Korate mill have coffee planted in high altitude zones nearby that span a range of 1900 - 2100 meters above sea level. They only produce dry processed coffees at this site ("naturals"), and with a capacity of up to 2 shipping containers a season (roughly 80k # of green coffee). That's a lot of coffee, however, it's actually on the small side for Ethiopia! The mill has registered more than 116 small farmers in total from the villages bordering the site, most with an average farm size of 2 hectares of coffee or less. Farmers are paid a higher rate for delivering only ripe cherries, which means less hand labor at the drying beds, and ultimately, a cleaner sorted coffee. Mill workers also mitigate unripe coffee by "floating" the coffee cherries in water. Generally, unripe coffee floats while the ripe coffee sinks. This makes removal quite easy, and a first step in grading. The coffee is then moved to raised drying beds for around 3 to 4 weeks time, until dried to around 11% moisture content.
detail.short_description: Korate shows very nice fruit tones in the cup, with shifting flavor profiles as it cools. Bittersweet tones underpin the cup, with dried peach, berry, mint, baking spices, red tea, pungent burnt sugar, dark chocolate truffle. City to Full City+.

overview_attrs.Cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids

detail.full_cupping_notes: The fragrance from this Hunapu lot smelled lightly sweetened with toasted sugar, nutty hints, and a nice cocoa dimension. Images of caramel and warming spices emerged in the steam after pouring hot water on the grounds, with an almond pastry note that brought to mind marzipan. City+ roasts were balanced and moderately sweet, accented by a light caramel glaze, chocolate chips and hints of creamy hazelnut and malted beer grains. The acidity level was pleasantly crisp, adding a faint zested orange note to my lighter roasts, and a bit like barley green tea in the aftertaste. The coffee produces some very nice chocolate roast tones, especially at Full City or darker. Our darkest roast was right around Full City (no 2nd Crack) and had very pleasant chocolate notes of Nutella chocolate-hazelnut spread, cocoa powder with cinnamon and a hint of smoked dark chocolate in the finish. Dark roasts still have a hint of acidity, but will work well as espresso nonetheless, as it has in previous years.
detail.farm_notes: Hunapu is the indigenous name for Volcan de Agua, not far from Antigua's main center where we buy nearly half our Guatemalan coffees each year. But this reach has expanded to several of the outlying areas thanks to the intermediary we work with, who also happens to be both a farmer and mill manager (and just about every other coffee related job title!). Unlike the "estate" coffees we're used to from Antigua, the Hunapu area is comprised of small scale farmers whose coffee fields are planted on the volcano's slopes across an altitude range of 1600 to 1900 meters above sea level. Roughly 450 farmers are currently selling their coffee to the mill in Antigua where each lot is assessed for quality, and separated accordingly. This is a micro-region separation from "Ciudad Vieja", made up mostly of cultivars Bourbon, Caturra, and Catuaí.
detail.short_description: Well-balanced, bittersweet brew, hints of caramel glaze, hazelnut-chocolate spread, and malted beer grains. Moderate acidity points to zested citrus and roasted barley tea. City+ to Full City+. Good for espresso.

overview_attrs.Cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Typica Types

detail.full_cupping_notes: Rosalio Villatoro's coffee offers balanced bittersweetness at a wide range of roast levels, with crowd-pleasing flavors of chocolate and nut. The fragrance and aroma show a bit of toffee and caramel in the sweetness, with tree nuts, and slight bittering scent of dark cocoa and burnt sugar. In the City+ to Full City range, the brewed coffee tastes like it's saturated with cocoa notes, like semi-sweet chocolate chips, lightly sweetened cocoa powder, chocolate biscotti, and more. The sweetness comes up a bit as it cools, dark toffee and caramelized sugars, with accents of almond, pistachio, and some walnut bittering in the aftertaste. I pick up on some slight herbal notes in the City+ roasts, along with a subtle lime-like acidity, that all but disappear at Full City or darker. Dark roasts will pair very well with cream if that's your preference, and will certainly double as a chocolatey shot of espresso.
detail.farm_notes: This coffee is from Rosalio Villatoro, one part of the Villatoro family whose coffees we've bought and blended as "Familia Villatoro" in the past, as well as offered on its own when there is enough. We thought this particular lot deserved being showcased outside of a blend, and is thankfully a sizable bag count! The Villatoro family lives in the Peña Blanca part of La Libertad, and their farms are situated around 1700 meters above sea level. They have mostly Bourbon and Caturra planted on their farms, with a sprinkling of Typica trees scattered throughout. This coffee comes to us through a joint-effort of a local micro-mill owner who is able to process and separate the micro-lots we approve, and a sophisticated dry mill where they handle the finishing touches for exportation of the green beans. It's also part of our "Proyecto Xinabajul" small holder project in the region, which you can read more about HERE .
detail.short_description: Balanced bittersweetness at a wide range of roasts, with crowd-pleasing flavors of chocolate and nuts. Flavors of toffee, semi-sweet chocolate chips, chocolate biscotti, almond and walnut. City+ to Full City+. Good for espresso.

specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 18+ screen - Monsoon coffee has been swelled with water and is a pale color, split, and with some minor defects like bug holes

detail.full_cupping_notes: There's nothing quite like Indian Monsooned coffee. It's all body, with intense, bittering roast flavors, and very low acidity. These aspects are what make it a go-to for so many espresso blends. In fact, it's a big part of the success of one of our most popular blends, Sweet Maria's Liquid Amber Espresso Blend . On its own, the cup is a bit of a shock to the palate. Much more bitter than sweet, caramel notes are merely hints brooding low tones. At Full City+ to French (FC+ should be the minimum), the cup has pungent bitter cocoa, unsweetened Baker's chocolate, spice, earthy accent notes, and a smokey aroma. The cup cools to interesting flavor accents like roasted corn, and earthy raw and roasted cacao nibs. Monsoon is for blending in our opinion, adding body and bittering low tones. It does not conform to standard cupping evaluation, and we added in a "cupper's correction" score of 8 to bump it up to 85 points as a way of expressing how we think this lot compares to other Monsoon coffees we've tried. It's an exotic flavor profile for sure, and perhaps an acquired taste. I recommend trying a very small amount at first to see if you like it, and also used sparingly for espresso blending - it will add quite a bit of crema and body to the shot.
detail.farm_notes: Monsooned coffees are stored in special warehouses until the Monsoon season comes around. The sides of the warehouse are opened and moist monsoon winds circulate around the coffee making it swell in size and take on a mellowed but aggressive flavor. The idea is that it recreates the conditions coffee was subjected to back when coffee was transported by clipper ships to Europe. This Monsooned Malabar is sourced from several farms in Southern India. Typically, the coffee is dry processed, then spread on the floor of the special warehouse, raked and turned around by hand to enable them to soak in moisture of the humid winds. The monsooning process takes around 3-6 months of duration, where in the beans swell to twice their original size and turn a pale golden color. Then they do additional rounds of hand sorting to remove any coffee that did not expand properly, and the coffee is prepared for export. This is an extremely pungent cup with a unique combination of burnt-bittering flavors, caramel finish and potent earthy aspects. It is not for those who like a "clean" cup, or sweet coffees! By all standard definitions, this is a defective set of cup flavors, though still quite interesting, unique, and not to mention, useful. (It's been a key component in our Liquid Amber espresso blend since the beginning!) Monsooned Malabar gets a pass from the coffee censors because of cultural tradition, history, and the fact that (while it doesn't conform to the traditional ideas of good coffee) it is in it's own right a unique coffee flavor. It has some use in espresso blending with a preparation of longer drum roasting and resting (after roasting) of 3+ days. There are Italian espresso roasting companies that use this coffee in their "exotic" blend offering, along with 2-3 other non-monsooned arabicas to even out the cup and provide aroma and some sweetness. Even as a drip/infusion brew, the coffee mellows after 2 days and the cup is more balanced so resting is key to best cup results. Please see the physical appearance of the coffee in that first photo, as it can be quite a shock if you've never seen Monsoon coffee before! It's pale white, slightly 'speckled'. We do our best to find the best quality all around, and think this is one of the cleaner looking lots we've seen.
detail.short_description: An interesting cup for fans of earthy, pungent roast tones, and low acid coffees. Dark roasting recommended, brings body and deep low tones to espresso blends (we use it in Liquid Amber!). Read full cup notes. Full City+ to French. Good for espresso blending.

detail.full_cupping_notes: Kinjo coffee piqued our interest for its origin as much as its flavor. It comes from Meru, a county clear on the other side of Mount Kenya from where we buy most of our Kenya's. It's where some of the first coffee was cultivated in Kenya, and you still see a lot of old SL-28 planted. Meru coffees have a unique flavor profile compared to Nyeri and Kirinyaga, with sweetness reminiscent of Burundi coffees, as well as subtle fruits and spices. This lot leads with notes of brown sugars in the cup, sucanat type natural sugars, unfolding to fruit accents of moderate intensity. I get a canned fruit element in flavor, like the sweet, syrupy aspects of canned plum that leaves behind a slight metallic tang on the palate. Fruits are well moderated compared to sweetness, and were mostly present in our lightest City roast. The acidity is berry-toned and fairly well integrated into the sweetness too. I get some strong tea bittering in the aftertaste that leads to rustic cocoa in the long finish. I didn't love my Full City roast brewed, but do like it as espresso. My ristretto shots had deep-toned chocolates and tart red fruits, and tasted like 80% dark chocolate juxtaposed by blackberry juice with a slightly puckering lemon note on the tip of your tongue. The finish is so long and bittering, like roasted cacao nibs. It's not the creamiest shot, but far from thin. Best solo, without milk.
detail.farm_notes: This is the first year we've purchased Kinjo, a coffee that comes from the opposite side of the mountain than our Nyeri's and Kirinyaga's. Meru County is home to the Meru people, a Bantu ethnic group who are said to be some of the first Africans to grow coffee in Kenya starting back in the early 1930's. We find the flavor profile of Meru coffee to be quite different than the bright coffees of Nyeri. The acidity tends to be more integrated into the sweetness, and the coffee can yield some very interesting dark fruit accents. Kinjo is a washing station - or "factory" as they're known in Kenya - named for the village it resides in. It is part of Katheri Farmers Cooperative Society, and operates as a conduit for local coffee farmers to sell their coffee and receive agronomical assistance as cooperative members. Altitude in this region ranges from 1650 meters to above 2000 meters above sea level in neighboring Katheri. Farmers typically have very small plots of coffee (less than half a hectare) and is one of several cash crops grown. You see a lot of old SL-28 planted around Meru too. This is an AB separation, which are the medium size coffee beans that measure 15/64" to 17/64" in size. Unless you're grading coffee, that's a pretty pretty difficult measurement to visualize! Imagine the size uniformity of a typical Guatemalan coffee. There is one grade size larger in Kenya, the AA, which commands the highest price but doesn't necessarily mean it cups any better than the AB. We found this lot to show some interesting dark fruit tones, with more moderate acidity compared to some of our Nyeri coffees.
detail.short_description: Leads with rustic sugar sweetness in the cup, cooling to moderate hints of fruits and well-integrated acidity. Date sugar, molasses, canned plum, bittering tea and cocoa finish. City to Full City. Good for espresso.

specs.Processing: Wet Process (Washed), the Swiss Water Process Decaf
specs.Appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 15-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination

detail.full_cupping_notes: The grinds let off a rustic sweetness, pungent coconut palm sugar, with accents of bran muffin, and spice cake. The wet aroma brought out more of the sweetness, as well as an interesting peppery aspect. This is a very versatile coffee in terms of roast level, with positive acidity for decaf coffee in the light roasts that can be tamped down with darker roast development. It offers balanced chocolate bittersweet tones between City and Full City, the lighter giving off flavors I associate with Indonesian coffees, like rice syrup, and herbal tarragon. There's a brisk citrus accent that fades to a peppery note of chipotle laced chocolate, and a clean finish that's a bit abrupt. Full City roasts are more bodied/bittersweet, with interesting cocoa/toasted grain profiles, like cocoa crisped rice, chocolate malted grain, and something like black sesame brownie. This should make outstanding espresso!
detail.farm_notes: Papua New Guinea occupies the Eastern half of the island it shares with the Indonesian province of Irian (no sizable coffee production comes from Irian). There can be a huge range of cups from Papua New Guinea, and the so-called Plantation coffees represent the cleaner character of the coffee produced on the island... more like a good Central American than part of the Indonesian profile. This decaf is a good representation of the balanced flavors you can find in Papua New Guinea, and quite versatile in terms of roast level and brew methods. The lot is comprised of the coffee from many small farms in Goroka, which is part of the very high altitude Eastern Highland region. Coffee grows between 1700 and 2000 meters above sea level, and the farms are typically less than 1 hectare on average. It was decaffeinated by the folks at Swiss Water Decaf in Vancouver, Canada. Their water-only process method removes 99.9% of the caffeine from coffee without any chemical solvents. As far as decaffeination goes, it's one of the gentler processes for the coffee and we find that we get a nice approximation of the non-decaf coffee that we send them.
detail.short_description: Versatile in the roaster, balanced chocolate tones and positive acidity for decaf coffee. Notes of rice syrup, tarragon, citrus, dark cocoa, chipotle and black sesame. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.

detail.full_cupping_notes: For anaerobic coffee, this lot packs more bittersweet intensity than fruit. We found it to have a bit more clarity in the cup too, with balanced flavors reminiscent of a traditional wet process coffee. The dry fragrance smells of molasses and other unrefined sugars, dark cocoa bittering, roasted almond and mild fruit accents. The wet aroma has potent chocolate roast tones in the steam, with faint hints of chocolate malt, rustic sugars and dried banana. Bittersweetness is very well-defined in the brewed coffee, like bean to bar chocolates made with a high percentage of cocoa solids, offering sweet relief up front that fades to long cocoa bittering aspects. Pungent roast flavors are hefty through to the finish, with contrasting hints of bittering tannic tea. Thick body punctuates the hefty flavors and adds to this coffee's all around substantial feel. Excellent espresso candidate.
detail.farm_notes: This is an anaerobic wet-process ("washed") coffee, meaning the coffee cherry was stored in sealed barrels for 2-3 days before being processed down to the seed and dried. The anaerobic process method tends to be associated with wild fruit flavors, but that's not what we find in Aulia's coffee. Instead, it delivers more on the bittersweet, hefty chocolate tones and body than anything else. Pak Aulia is both a coffee farmer and "collector", meaning he works as a sort of middle man who buys whole cherry and wet parchment from farmers in the surrounding regions (typically Bebesen and Kute Panang, near his home). Aulia manages some of his own processing at the small mill he's set up at his home. With small scale comes the capability for a high level of quality management, which he puts into all of the different process techniques he employs (including wet process and wet hulled, honey and dry process too). He also processes some of his coffee at a new mill nearby who have modern machinery to process coffee well, and plenty of space to store it. The coffee is then moved to a dry mill in Tekengon, where it undergoes intensive hand sorting to clean up to Grade 1 standards. That extra care and attention given to quality control is apparent when you look at the green coffee, and of course in flavor too, though not without defects.
detail.short_description: For anaerobic coffee, this lot packs more bittersweet intensity than fruit. Brews balanced flavors and thick body, pungent roast tones, bean to bar chocolate, tannic tea, very long finish. City+ to Full City+. Good for espresso.
